title_zh: Michael Moritz：40 年投资与写作的教训
subtitle_zh: Sequoia 传奇投资人 Michael Moritz 回望家族史与局外人驱动力，谈 Iacocca、Steve Jobs、Ferguson、独狂式创造与 AI 时代。
summary_zh: 本期 Invest Like the Best 中，Patrick O'Shaughnessy 对话 Sequoia 传奇投资人、记者出身的 Michael Moritz，围绕他新书对家族史的追溯展开，核心问题是“一个人到哪里结束、下一个人在哪里开始”。Moritz 说写这本书最大的意外收获是终于弄清自己是谁、为何成为现在的样子。他的父母三十年代从纳粹德国逃到威尔士，是难民而非集中营幸存者，始终不愿用“幸存者”一词；他强调少数者是一种内心感受。那种不顾一切也要活下去的底色给了他靠机智吃饭的本能：对他人动机高度怀疑，预先琢磨坏事会怎样发生并加以防范，也赋予他当时并不自知的韧劲与狠劲。他特别指出这些印记不是通过故事传递的，父母只讲粗线条、从不谈细节，而是通过日常举止与“大难并不遥远”的气氛；十二三岁之前吸收进来的东西，无论天使还是恶魔，都要带着过完余生。最深的悔意是让父母蒙羞。转到投资，他说最喜欢的投资就是 Sequoia 本身：1995 年接手时第一条念头是别把它搞砸，第二条是确保每个人都相信“我们只和下一笔投资一样好”。节目还穿插他为一位跨行业成就惊人却颇具争议的人物发出的 gobsmacked 式赞叹，以及记者训练留给他的手艺：把事情蒸馏到本质、保持极短；他借此谈词汇量的力量，指 Trump 的常用词汇约 2,400 个、在历任美国总统中遥遥垫底，而 Obama 约 4,500 个，庞大的词汇库才能让人用简单方式表达复杂想法。收束于他异常低的自我评价与“母亲的幽灵”：她唤起他对艺术的兴趣，却永远会挑毛病。

turns.en: To learn more, visit psum.vc. When I was reading your book, one of the lines or the ideas that has really stuck with me ever since is, where does one person end and the next person begin?
turns.zh: 了解更多请访问 psum.vc。我读你那本书的时候，有一句话、一个想法，从那以后一直留在我心里：一个人到哪里结束，下一个人在哪里开始？

turns.en: And this deep dive that you took into the impact of one's history, family history, heritage on who a person is. I'm interested in this from so many angles as a parent, as a person interested in history, as a person interested in genetics, nature versus nurture.
turns.zh: 你深入探究了一个人的家族史、传承对其为人的影响。我从太多角度对这件事感兴趣：作为父母，作为对历史感兴趣的人，作为对遗传学、天性与教养（nature versus nurture）感兴趣的人。

turns.en: If I were to sum up the book in that question, what is your answer to that? What did you come away thinking after this deep study of your own family's history?
turns.zh: 如果让我用那个问题来概括这本书，你的答案是什么？在如此深入地区研究自己家族的历史之后，你最终的思考是什么？

turns.en: One of the things that came out of the book, which I didn't really expect, was discovering who I am and why I became whatever it is that I've become.
turns.zh: 这本书写出后有一个连我自己都没料到的收获，就是发现了我是谁、我为什么会成为现在这个样子。

turns.en: And that was an unexpected gift of the writing. And it came from this exploration of my family's past, in particular, my parents. Going back and excavating the deep memories of childhood, the sort of atmosphere in our home and in the general new year in which I grew up, helped me understand a lot about why I am who I am and react to certain things in the fashion that I do.
turns.zh: 那是写作带来的一份意外馈赠。它来自对我家族往事的探索，尤其是对我父母的探寻。回头去发掘童年深处的记忆，去还原我们家里、以及我成长的那个世界里的整体氛围，帮我理解了很多：我为什么是现在这个样子，为什么以这样的方式对某些事情做出反应。

turns.en: Because unwittingly, obviously, every parent leaves an imprint on a child. That's obviously especially true during the formative years. Whatever the formative years are, I'm no sort of child specialist or scientist.
turns.zh: 因为每一位父母都会在不知不觉中给孩子留下印记，这显然在塑造人格的年头里尤为如此。至于塑造人格的年头到底是几岁，我又不是儿童专家或科学家。

turns.en: Before you turn 12, 13, 14 years old, those imprints that you've absorbed in some manner, consciously or unconsciously, those remain with you.
turns.zh: 在你满十二、十三、十四岁之前，那些以某种方式、无论有意识还是无意识地吸收进来的印记，都会留在你身上。

turns.en: And both the angels and demons, I think, that you deal with for the rest of your life. What were yours? I'm so curious that you're performing on yourself the exercise that you're famous for doing with others that you invested in or hired, focusing on these first 14 years.
turns.zh: 我想，无论是天使还是恶魔，你都得带着它们过完余生。你的天使和恶魔是什么？我特别好奇：你把你那套闻名于外的方法用在了自己身上——就是你审视你投资过、雇佣过的那些人的方法，聚焦头十四年。

turns.en: What new understanding of yourself came out of this exercise? I grew up in this family of refugees from Nazi Germany and Wales. Refugees by definition are a minority.
turns.zh: 从这次自我审视里，你对自己有什么新的认识？我成长于一个难民家庭，父母从纳粹德国逃到威尔士。难民，按定义就是少数。

turns.en: Jewish refugees in Wales during the 1960s and 1970s were a further minority. People look at me today and they think, oh, here's this old white man, he's not a minority.
turns.zh: 六十年代和七十年代威尔士的犹太难民，更是少数中的少数。今天人们看着我，会想：哦，这就是个白人老头，不是什么少数群体。

turns.en: And I can understand that, but it's how an individual feels rather than how other people might look at you. It touched me in a variety of ways.
turns.zh: 我能理解别人这么看，但一个少数者是自己内心如何感受，而不是别人怎么看你。这段经历在很多层面都触动了我。

turns.en: My parents, they were never in the camps, they got out of Germany in the 1930s. And they were loath to use the word survivor because they always felt the word survivor denoted somebody who actually had survived the camps, but they were refugees and in their own way had survived.
turns.zh: 我父母从来没有进过集中营，他们三十年代就离开了德国。他们很不愿用“幸存者”这个词，因为他们一直认为幸存者指的是真正从集中营里活下来的人；但他们是难民，也以他们自己的方式幸存了下来。

turns.en: That motive to survive no matter what the odds were, even though the odds that I faced growing up weren't like my parents, I think the need to survive.
turns.zh: 那种不顾一切也要活下去的冲动——尽管我成长过程中面临的处境和父母当年完全不同——我想，根子还是生存的需要。

turns.en: When you think about surviving, you're thinking about, to some extent, living by your wits, being very suspicious of the motives of others, wondering where and how bad things will occur and happen and guard against them.
turns.zh: 当你想着生存，某种程度上你就是在靠机智吃饭：对别人的动机高度怀疑，琢磨坏事会在哪里、以什么方式发生，并加以防范。

turns.en: I think it gave me in retrospect, I didn't understand it at the time, a sort of drive-in grit that I wouldn't have had without that particular atmospheric backdrop.
turns.zh: 事后回想，我觉得那股背景气氛赋予了我一种韧劲和狠劲；当时我并不自知，但如果没有那种氛围底色，我是不会有它的。

turns.en: When you study it and you think about your own childhood, how did that transfer from your parents to you? Was it the stories they told? It was definitely not the stories they told because they didn't tell the stories.
turns.zh: 当你回头研究这些、审视自己的童年，那种气质是怎么从父母传递到你身上的？是他们讲的故事吗？肯定不是他们讲的故事，因为他们根本没讲。

turns.en: I didn't really get to know the stories until I sat down and began work on this book. What I did know was the general arc of history, obviously, this miserable, ferocious, catastrophic whirlwind in which they and millions of others were caught up, but they didn't talk about the past in the real detail that I much later, when I was thinking about the book, became interested in.
turns.zh: 我是在坐下来开始写这本书的时候，才真正了解到那些故事的。我过去知道的只是历史的大致轮廓：那场吞噬了他们和数百万人的可怕、凶猛、毁灭性的风暴——但他们从不以真正的细节谈过去，而恰恰是那些细节，是我后来构思这本书时最想知道的。

turns.en: It was just broad sweeps. I think it was much more the daily behavior, the reaction to events, the reaction to things, the sense that doom was not very far away.
turns.zh: 他们讲的只是粗线条。我想，更多传递下来的是日常的举止、对事件的反应、对万物的态度，以及那种“大难并不遥远”的感觉。

turns.en: The fact that if horrors had occurred in the past, there was a real need to be vigilant and wary about navigating daily life. There was a couple of stories in the book, one in particular where you talk about two separate people, one who decided to stay in Germany and one who decided to leave.
turns.zh: 既然过去曾经发生过恐怖之事，那你就真的需要在日常生活里保持警惕、小心周旋应对。书里有两个人的故事，其中一段你讲到两个不同的人，一个决定留在德国，一个决定离开。

turns.en: Quite a poignant and interesting on this topic of survivor or outsider, early instinct when things are changing to take notice and not double down and stick around.
turns.zh: 关于幸存者或局外人这个话题，这非常令人感慨、也非常有意思：当环境开始变化时，早期的本能是有所察觉，而不是加倍押注、赖着不走。

turns.en: Maybe tell that story and explain what you learned. The two individuals, Patrick, that you refer to were my grandfathers, my maternal grandfather and my paternal grandfather.
turns.zh: 能讲讲那个故事、说说你学到了什么吗？Patrick，你说到的那两个人是我的两位祖父，我外祖父和我祖父。

turns.en: I'll start with my paternal grandfather, who was a civil servant. He was a lower level judge in the judiciary in Bavaria, a province in southern Germany.
turns.zh: 我先说父系祖父，他是一名文官，在巴伐利亚——德国南部的一个州——当过初级法官。

turns.en: He had fought in World War I. He had somehow or other survived the horror of Verdun. He had been given his iron cross and he was, I think, a great believer in the German state, in the security that the state offered.
turns.zh: 他参加过第一次世界大战，不知怎么竟从凡尔登的恐怖中活了下来，被授予铁十字勋章。我认为他对德国国家、对国家能提供的保障深信不疑。

turns.en: And then much later in 1933, he lost his job. This is my assessment of the situation because he was a civil servant. He was by nature conservative, by nature somewhat cautious, but also had this great belief in the state and the endurance of the state and the durability of the state and that eventually the storm would blow over.
turns.zh: 然后在 1933 年，他丢了工作。以上是我对局势的判断：他是文官，天性保守，天性有些谨慎，但他对国家、对国家的延续性和持久力怀有坚定的信念，相信风暴终会过去。

turns.en: He also had a pension and the pension was very important to him as a means for survival. It was a combination of all of those things. He wasn't oblivious, obviously, to what was happening around him, but it did make him more reluctant to leave Germany, I think, until it was too late.
turns.zh: 他还有退休金，而退休金对他这样求生存的人来说至关重要。是这一切叠加在一起。他对周围发生的事显然并不麻木，但我想，正是这些让他迟迟不愿离开德国，直到为时已晚。

turns.en: And people forget, even if somebody had decided to leave Germany, there are all sorts of obstacles in the way. You had to find a place elsewhere that would accept you.
turns.zh: 人们会忘记，即使一个人决定离开德国，也是一路障碍：你得找到一个愿意接纳你的地方。

turns.en: You had to pay big taxes to the Nazi government in order to be able to secure your exit visa. So they're all these sorts of obstacles. So that was my paternal grandfather.
turns.zh: 你还得向纳粹政府缴纳高额税款，才能拿到出境许可。所以到处是这样的障碍。这是我的父系祖父。

turns.en: He and his wife eventually were shipped off east and disappeared from history. My maternal grandfather was cut from a different cloth. I was too callous as a youth to really understand this, but he died when I was about 16.
turns.zh: 他和祖母最终被押送向东，从此消失在历史之中。我的母系祖父则完全是另一种质地。我年轻时太没心没肺，并不真正懂得这一点。他在我大约十六岁那年去世了。

turns.en: He had been a cattle trader, which was one of the occupations that Jews were really permitted to do in Germany, but he was almost blind as a young man and completely blind by the time that I met him.
turns.zh: 他生前做牲口贩子，那是当时德国犹太人几乎唯一被允许从事的职业之一。但他年轻时眼睛就几乎失明，到我认识他时已经完全看不见了。

turns.en: But somehow or other had been able to carve out a comfortable living for himself and his family by trading in cattle in the rural village in northwestern Germany.
turns.zh: 可不知怎么，他硬是在德国西北部一个乡村靠贩运牲口为自己和家人挣出了一份安稳日子。

turns.en: My assessment of him in retrospect was that he was more streetwise. He was more entrepreneurial, wasn't burdened by the need to remain and collect a state pension because he'd always been able to sustain himself and look out for his future.
turns.zh: 事后回想，我对他的评价是：他更懂街头智慧，更有企业家精神，也没有那种必须留下来领国家退休金的牵绊，因为他一直有能力自谋生路、为自己打算。

turns.en: And he got out with his wife, my grandmother, but they got out by the skin of their teeth. They got out 72 hours before war broke out. 72 hours later, they too would have perished.
turns.zh: 他和我的外祖母成功逃了出去，但真是千钧一发。他们是在开战前七十二小时离开的。再晚七十二小时，他们也会丧命。

turns.en: What do you take from that? What is the big lesson from that instinct? How does that instinct imprinted on you and on the people you back throughout your life and career written about?
turns.zh: 你从中汲取了什么？这个本能带来的是什么大教训？这个本能如何铭刻在你身上，又如何影响你这一生长河里支持、合作和书写过的人们？

turns.en: I'm not sure that it's all that relevant to the people I've encountered in this journey through life, but it certainly has had consequences for me, particularly in times like the ones that we are living through at the moment and the atmosphere that is prevalent to some extent in the US and also in Western Europe.
turns.zh: 我不确定这对这一路人生里我遇到的人是否都那么有直接相关性，但对我自己，它确实产生了后果，尤其是在我们正生活的这样的时代，以及某种程度在美国和西欧都弥漫的那种氛围里。

turns.en: I think the necessity for always feeling that you have a bolt hole, that you have some place to go if the fire gets too hot. That's the lesson that I took away from my family history, clearly saying that you can never have enough passports.
turns.zh: 我觉得，永远要觉得自己有一个应急藏身处（bolt hole），有一个万一火势太猛时可以去的地方。这就是我从家族历史里学到的教训——难怪人们常说，护照永远不嫌多。

turns.en: Do you feel that especially true now? Say a bit about the state of the world, how you perceive the state of the world. It's an uncomfortable place for minorities.
turns.zh: 你现在尤其有这样的感觉吗？谈谈你对当今世界的看法吧。

turns.en: The United States and Western Europe writ large. It doesn't matter whether you're Asian or Muslim or black or Jewish. I understand the reasons and I want to be careful as well.
turns.zh: 对少数群体来说，这个世界让人不安，美国以及整个西欧都是如此。无论你是亚裔、穆斯林、黑人还是犹太人。我理解背后的原因，我也想谨慎措辞。

turns.en: I am not whining about anti-Semitism. I'm not complaining about it. I long ago came to terms with the fact that it's just a fact of life. It's been around for 2,500 years.
turns.zh: 我不是在为反犹主义哭诉，也不是在抱怨它。我很早就已经接受了这个事实：它就是一种生活常态，已经存在了两千五百年。

turns.en: It's not going to disappear in 2026 or 2030. It's always going to be with us. In fact, as we were talking about a few minutes ago, I think the fact that anti-Semitism was around and has been around and it's been something I've been conscious of all my life or all my sentient life, it's made me stronger.
turns.zh: 它不会在 2026 年或 2030 年消失，它会永远和我们同在。事实上，就像我们几分钟前聊到的，反犹主义一直存在、我也一直有清醒的意识——在我整个有感知的人生里都如此——它反而让我更强大了。

turns.en: I think it's disquieting if you're living in a society where in America, I think my simplistic way of thinking about who feels safe is the contingent of Americans who feel safe are white Christians who own guns.
turns.zh: 如果你生活在美国这样的社会，那景象是令人不安的。我看待“谁感到安全”的方式很简单：在美国，觉得自己安全的群体，是拥有枪支的白人基督徒。

turns.en: Everybody else feels a degree of insecurity, whether you're pursued by ICE or you go to a house of prayer that has to be guarded by police to ensure that that's safe and that exists in America.
turns.zh: 其他人都有一定程度的不安全感：你可能被 ICE 追缉，你可能要去一座必须由警察站岗守卫才能确保安全的神殿礼拜——而这就是美国当下的现实。

turns.en: It exists in the United Kingdom, in France, in other countries around Europe where far-right governments have come to the fore and obviously everybody has read about the recent elections in Germany of a far-right party in Saxony province.
turns.zh: 这样的现实也存在于英国、法国以及欧洲其他国家，极右翼势力正在抬头；显然大家也都看到了德国萨克森州最近选举中极右翼政党的表现。

turns.en: I think in times of economic distress where you have millions of people who've been tens of millions of people who feel they've been left behind, that feeling of despair can easily be whipped up into a horrendous stew by leaders with authoritarian impulses.
turns.zh: 我认为，在经济困顿的时刻，当有千万人觉得自己被抛在时代后面，那种绝望感很容易被带有威权冲动的领导人搅成一锅可怕的乱流。

turns.en: You're fortunate to put on your optimistic or hopeful hat and thinking about the future as it relates to this problem. Well, Victor Orban was booted from office.
turns.zh: 你也很幸运，能戴上乐观或希望的帽子，去思考与此相关的未来。你看，Victor Orban 刚刚被选民赶下了台。

turns.en: He was riding high a couple of years ago in some places that clearly are pushes to the center, which would be, I think, very consoling for people and a return to some modicum of civility in the various societies in which people like us travel.
turns.zh: 几年前他在很多地方还风光无限。那些明显向中间回摆的力量，我想会让人们得到宽慰，也会让我们这些人往来的各个社会重新找回一点体面。

turns.en: So here in America, clearly the midterms of the next 18 months after that are really going to shape how we're going to live in the next decade because there's been the imprint of one person on the last decade in America, I think in Britain, the person who's identified with the far-right Nigel Farage may well have had his best day and his best day may well be behind him.
turns.zh: 所以在我们美国，显然十八个月之后的中期选举，将真正决定我们接下来十年怎么生活，因为过去十年，美国被一个人的印记深深压过。我觉得在英国，与极右翼挂钩的 Nigel Farage 可能已经过了他最好的日子，而他最好的日子很可能已经过去了。

turns.en: I think it's different in France with Marie Le Pen and the elections next year. It's different in Spain and it's potentially different in Germany.
turns.zh: 在法国，有 Marine Le Pen 和明年的选举，情况不一样；西班牙不一样，德国也可能不一样。

turns.en: Do you think that the internet fundamentally changes the potential for civility and political moderation because it's so rewards, extremes, and attention?
turns.zh: 你觉得互联网从根本上改变了体面与政治温和的可能性吗？因为它如此奖励极端、奖励注意力？

turns.en: I think the three-letter answer is yes. I think it's been true of every form of new media from the beginning of the printing press. But obviously, the internet in the mobile telephony has made it far easier to spread false memes in Uendo, but it's a much larger, more amplified version of what occurred in Germany when radio took off during the 1930s and where the radio waves were dominated by extreme propaganda and racist views and loud lies told frequently.
turns.zh: 我想三个字的答案是：会。我认为对自印刷机问世以来每一种新媒介都是如此。但显然，互联网和移动通信让虚假模因（memes）更容易、更快地传播。它是 1930 年代广播在德国兴起时所发生之事的一个放大无数倍的版本——那时电波被极端宣传和种族主义观点占据，大声的谎言被一遍遍播放。
